To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spectral coefficients of an arbitrary switching function can be computed in terms of a real transform of the switching function and that the inverse transform can also be carried out by the same means.

the spectral coefficients of an n-variable switching function are given by the sum of all possible products of n real variables, each variable appearing in the product with a weight of either 0 or 1; the weight of a variable is 0 if it is a don’t care in any of the minterms that define the function, and 1 otherwise; the number of products is 2^n-2; and the number of real variables appearing in a product is at most n.

the real transform of a switching function, and its inverse transform, are both computable in a complexity which is less than the minterm expansion of the function, and which is also less than the complexity of the minimal sum-of-products representation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spectral coefficients of Boolean functions and the computation of the inverse transform.
a class of Boolean functions that can be expressed in a disjoint sum-of-product representation.
the spectral analysis and synthesis of switching functions in the real transform domain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spectral domain is a very useful domain for switching function representation and manipulation.
the proposed approach is an alternative to the conventional spectral methods for computing the spectral coefficients and for the inverse transform.
the spectral coefficients of the function can be efficiently computed from the real transform, and the real transform can be efficiently computed in turn from the function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spectral domain is a very useful domain for the study of switching functions, and that the real transform is an efficient mechanism for the computation in the spectral domain.
a switching function can be expressed in terms of its spectral coefficients and the inverse transform is a linear operation in these coefficients.

a switching function can be transformed into a disjoint sum-of-product representation of a complexity comparable to that of the minterm expansion of the function, and that the spectral coefficients can be computed in terms of this sum-of-product representation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spectral coefficients of the function can be computed from the real transform of a switching function in a way which is significantly more efficient than the minterm expansion method.
spectral analysis of switching functions is a viable alternative to the traditional algebraic approach.
spectral methods are not only useful for switching function analysis but can also be applied to switching function synthesis.
